subject: Caution: predict() expects categorical covariates in alphabetical order

messages.author: 3db91132d08e7572
messages.subject: Caution: predict() expects categorical covariates in alphabetical order
parts:
Unmarked:

I'm writing to report a potential caution in using the predict() function to calculate parameter estimates for categorical covariates.

I'm running an occupancy model with three different levels for 'guild' as a factor:
In alphabetical order, the three levels are HI for high, LO for low, and SE for severe.

> (m3 <- occu(~ guild ~ guild, data = plant.data))

Call:
occu(formula = ~guild ~ guild, data = plant.data)

Occupancy:
            Estimate    SE       z P(>|z|)
(Intercept)  -0.1484 0.539 -0.2751   0.783
guildLO       0.0792 1.019  0.0777   0.938
guildSE      -0.3122 0.551 -0.5666   0.571

Detection:
            Estimate    SE     z  P(>|z|)
(Intercept)   -1.432 0.374 -3.83 1.29e-04
guildLO       -0.663 0.637 -1.04 2.98e-01
guildSE        1.741 0.401  4.34 1.41e-05

AIC: 2358.34 
> # get estimates of occupancy and detection
> newdat <- data.frame(guild=c("LO", "HI", "SE"))
> (occ = predict(m3, type = "state", newdata=newdat, append=T)) # occupancy
  Predicted        SE     lower     upper guild
1 0.4826926 0.2157427 0.1464553 0.8353686    LO
2 0.4629645 0.1341344 0.2304433 0.7127919    HI
3 0.3868362 0.0266049 0.3361563 0.4400915    SE
> (det = predict(m3, type="det", newdata=newdat, append=T))  # detection
  Predicted         SE      lower     upper guild
1 0.1095911 0.05027051 0.04291649 0.2525204    LO
2 0.1927731 0.05820791 0.10291630 0.3320453    HI
3 0.5765125 0.03516806 0.50653699 0.6435479    SE

I can double-check calculations for backtransforming the estimates for HI, LO, and SE, and get the same answers.

> logit2prob <- function(logit){
+   odds <- exp(logit)
+   prob <- odds / (1 + odds)
+   return(prob)
+ }
> logit2prob(-1.432)
[1] 0.1927873
> logit2prob(-1.432-0.663)
[1] 0.1095837
> logit2prob(-1.432+1.741)
[1] 0.5766412

My factors were out of order so changed the order of the levels which gives me a model with different coefficients but the same AIC

> # reorder LO < HI < SE
> AllCombo$guild = factor(AllCombo$guild,levels(AllCombo$guild)[c(2,1,3)])
> # double check
> levels(AllCombo$guild)
[1] "LO" "HI" "SE"

> (m3 <- occu(~ guild ~ guild, data = plant.data))

Call:
occu(formula = ~guild ~ guild, data = plant.data)

Occupancy:
            Estimate    SE       z P(>|z|)
(Intercept)  -0.0692 0.864 -0.0800   0.936
guildHI      -0.0792 1.019 -0.0778   0.938
guildSE      -0.3915 0.871 -0.4493   0.653

Detection:
            Estimate    SE     z  P(>|z|)
(Intercept)   -2.095 0.515 -4.07 4.78e-05
guildHI        0.663 0.637  1.04 2.98e-01
guildSE        2.403 0.535  4.49 7.03e-06

AIC: 2358.34 

Again, I can generate the same parameter estimates for HI, LO, and SE by backtransforming from the new coefficients:

> logit2prob(-2.095+0.663)
[1] 0.1927873
> logit2prob(-2.095)
[1] 0.1095837
> logit2prob(-2.095+2.403)
[1] 0.576397

A problem arises if I try to use the predict() function to generate the parameter estimates with this model.
If I use the same string of levels for guild with this model, the parameter estimates are then mislabeled in the output.
Based on the calculations above, the LO guild should have a p of 0.109 and the HI guild should have a p of 0.192

> # get estimates of occupancy and detection
> newdat <- data.frame(guild=c("LO", "HI", "SE"))
> (occ = predict(m3, type = "state", newdata=newdat, append=T)) # occupancy
  Predicted         SE     lower     upper guild
1 0.4629701 0.13413883 0.2304415 0.7128032    LO
2 0.4827161 0.21577631 0.1464347 0.8354170    HI
3 0.3868353 0.02660479 0.3361556 0.4400903    SE
> (det = predict(m3, type="det", newdata=newdat, append=T))  # detection
  Predicted         SE      lower     upper guild
1 0.1927711 0.05820847 0.10291395 0.3320453    LO
2 0.1095866 0.05027361 0.04291053 0.2525304    HI
3 0.5765139 0.03516797 0.50653852 0.6435491    SE

It looks like the predict() function is expecting the levels of the factor to be sorted it alphabetically.  It is not actually matching the different levels of the factors to the coefficients. 
If you create a string of variables that are not in the input file, the predict() function will still generate and label parameter estimates.

> newdat <- data.frame(guild=c("Andy", "Marc", "Richard"))
> (occ = predict(m3, type = "state", newdata=newdat, append=T)) # occupancy
  Predicted         SE     lower     upper   guild
1 0.4827161 0.21577631 0.1464347 0.8354170    Andy
2 0.4629701 0.13413883 0.2304415 0.7128032    Marc
3 0.3868353 0.02660479 0.3361556 0.4400903 Richard
> (det = predict(m3, type="det", newdata=newdat, append=T))  # detection
  Predicted         SE      lower     upper   guild
1 0.1095866 0.05027361 0.04291053 0.2525304    Andy
2 0.1927711 0.05820847 0.10291395 0.3320453    Marc
3 0.5765139 0.03516797 0.50653852 0.6435491 Richard

A caution:  If you reorder the levels of a categorical covariate before you fit a model, the parameter estimates in your output might be mislabeled.

Regards, Brett.

Brett K. Sandercock
EM: brett.sa...@nina.no

messages.author: 4e956cc50ac3e075
messages.subject: RE: [unmarked] Caution: predict() expects categorical covariates in alphabetical order
parts:
Hi Brett,


this is a very good point. To make predictions from a data.frame( ), you need to use a data.frame where the variables are of the same type and use the same coding as your original data set used in the analysis. For instance, in your second example, you reordered the factor level to use LO as the reference level.


As a result, when you create your data set:

R uses HI as the reference level as the default contrast coding:

> levels(newdat$guild)
[1] "HI" "LO" "SE"


To ensure that the factors are coded in the same way, it is safer to use:

> newdat <- data.frame(guild = factor(c("LO", "HI", "SE"), levels = levels(plant.data$siteCovs$guild))


This should ensure that the predictions are consistent with the coding used in your model.


Best,


Marc

Hi Brett,

I think we should view this as a bug, and I'll try to fix it soon. Marc is correct about the reason why this is happening, and I second his recommendation for avoiding the problem. However, users shouldn't have to jump through such hoops to get what they want. I'll let people know if I'm able to fix the problem.

Thanks,
Richard
